ABSTRACT  
Activated carbon (AC) obtained by the pyrolysis of reed residue waste has been investigated for its potential 
application as a high-performance electrode material in supercapacitors. Four different pyrolysis temperatures 
(500, 600, 700, and 800 
◦
C) were implemented, and the optimum pyrolysis temperature was determined on the 
basis of the physicochemical properties and electrochemical measurements of the AC materials. AC obtained at a 
relatively low pyrolysis temperature of 600 
◦
C (denoted as C/600 
◦
C) presented a Hemistepta lyrata (bunge 
flower)-like porous nanostructure with a high specific surface area of 2074.72 m
2 
g
� 1 
and a large pore volume of 
0.930 cm
3 
g
� 1
. SEM and Raman spectroscopy have been used to inspect the surface morphology and assess the 
degree of graphitization of the AC materials. Electrochemical performances have been assessed by cyclic vol -
tammetry, galvanostatic charge/discharge, and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy. Sample C/600 
◦
C 
displayed a relatively large capacitance of 228 F g
� 1 
at a current density of 1 A g
� 1 
in 6 M KOH as the electrolyte, 
and it retained very good cyclic stability with a capacitance retention of 98.1% after 8000 cycles at a current 
density of 5.0 A g
� 1
. The results imply that C/600 
◦
C derived from reed residue waste constitutes a promising 
electrochemical supercapacitor electrode material.   
1. Introduction 
Non-renewable resources and energy sources such as oil and coal are 
becoming increasingly depleted because of the rapid development of the 
social economy. At the same time, environmental issues such as various 
exhaust gases and the greenhouse effect caused by these energy sources 
have become a global source of concern and an increasingly serious 
social issue. In the last decade, the energy crisis and environmental 
protection issues have intensified, and the demand for new energy 
sources and feasible environmental protection measures has grown. To 
meet the ever-increasing demand for efficient energy storage and envi -
ronmental pressures, it is urgent to seek sustainable clean energy 
generated from renewable resources [ 1 – 6 ]. Among various energy 
transformation and storage devices, supercapacitors (SCs), also known 
as ultracapacitors, have attracted great attention due to their higher 
power delivery ( > 10 kW kg
� 1
) and longer cycling life ( > 100,000 cycles) 
compared to batteries, simple principle, and safe operation [ 1 ]. There -
fore, SCs have been widely studied and developed in many fields in 
recent years, such as uninterruptible power supplies, portable consumer 
electronic devices, electric vehicles, industrial power and energy man -
agement, and load-levelling [ 4 , 7 , 8 ]. 
Generally, electrical double-layer capacitors (EDLCs) and pseudo -
capacitors are categorized as supercapacitors based on their charge- 
storage mechanisms. Energy is stored in EDLCs through the reversible 
adsorption of electrolyte ions on an active material; therefore, the 
capacitance of an EDLC relies heavily on the surface area of the electrode 
material and pore framework (porosity and size distribution), which 
needs to facilitate the access of electrolyte ions [ 9 ]. Unlike EDLCs, 
pseudocapacitors achieve energy storage through fast and reversible 
faradaic redox reactions, which take place at or near the electrode sur -
face. To meet the needs of high-energy supercapacitors, the choice of 
pseudocapacitive material with electro-active species is crucial to

generate high charge and to store charge within a short time [ 9 ]. The 
two mechanisms can work together simultaneously according to the 
nature of the electrode materials. 
It is widely acknowledged that the electrode material is one of the 
most important factors influencing supercapacitor performance. A large 
number of carbon-based electrode materials, such as AC [ 10 – 12 ], mes -
oporous carbon [ 13 – 15 ], graphene [ 16 – 18 ], carbon nanofibers [ 19 , 20 ], 
carbon nanotubes [ 21 , 22 ], xerogels [ 23 – 27 ], and carbide-derived car -
bons [ 28 – 30 ], have been widely explored by scholars. Among these 
carbon-based electrode materials, AC is widely used as an EDLC elec -
trode material due to its high specific surface area, somewhat control -
lable pore size distribution, excellent electrical conductivity, high 
physicochemical stability, high mechanical strength, high chemical 
polarity, and moderate cost. Historically, most commercial AC materials 
have been produced from petroleum residues, coal, peat, lignite, and so 
on. However, these limited and non-renewable precursors are clearly 
associated with high production costs and much environmental pollu -
tion. Hence, researchers have turned their attention to developing 
biomass-derived AC materials due to the abundance, low cost, and 
renewable and eco-friendly nature of such sources [ 31 ]. 
Giant reed, also known as Phragmites communis , Phragmites australis , 
or Arundo donax Linn, is a perennial, rhizomatous, and herbaceous plant 
of the Poaceae family distributed globally in Asia and the Mediterranean 
regions of North Africa, southern Europe, and the Middle East [ 32 , 33 ]. 
Because of its rapid growth, strong capacity to adapt to different envi -
ronments, and low input requirements, the biomass productivity of giant 
reed can reach 30 – 40 t/ha, which makes it a low-cost and sustainable 
feedstock for the production of biofuels, chemicals, and bioenergy [ 33 , 
34 ]. However, most of the biomass residues generated from giant reed 
every year are burnt on site, which results in serious environmental 
pollution and a waste of biomass resources. Fortunately, in the last few 
decades, some studies have been conducted to explore the application of 
AC derived from giant reed through physical activation (CO

on utilization of the waste residue that remains after extraction of the 
water-soluble chemical components, such as glucose, sucrose, and

extracted reed (reed residue waste) has been used as a precursor. AC 
materials have been prepared at different pyrolysis temperatures and 
then chemically activated with KOH. The influence of pyrolysis tem -
perature on the electrochemical performances of the as-prepared AC 
materials as supercapacitor electrodes has been studied. 
2. Experimental 
2.1. Materials 
Reed residue waste was purchased from Shengquan Group (Jinan, 
China). Potassium hydroxide (KOH) was purchased from Aladdin re -
agent Co., Ltd. (China). All chemical reagents were used as received 
without further purification. 
2.2. Synthesis of AC materials 
Reed residue waste was placed in a quartz tube furnace and heated at 
a rate of 10 
◦
C min
� 1 
to 500, 600, 700, or 800 
◦
C under a flow of N
2 
at 
200 mL min
� 1 
and maintained at the final temperature for 2 h. The as- 
prepared carbonization products were mixed with KOH, placed in a 
tubular furnace, and again heated at a rate of 10 
◦
C min
� 1 
under N
2 
at a 
flow rate of 200 mL min
� 1 
and maintained at the final temperature of 
800 
◦
C for 2 h. The mass ratio of as-prepared carbonization product to 
KOH was 1:5. The obtained products were washed with deionized water 
until the washings were neutral, and then dried in a vacuum oven at 
70 
◦
C for 24 h. The samples are denoted as C/500 
◦
C, C/600 
◦
C, C/ 
700 
◦
C, and C/800 
◦
C, respectively. 
2.3. Characterization of the AC materials 
The properties of the AC samples were determined by applying a 
series of topographic analysis methods. N
2 
adsorption/desorption iso -
therms were recorded at 77 K on a Micromeritics ASAP 2020 analyzer. 
The specific surface areas and pore volumes of the AC samples were 
determined through Brunauer – Emmett – Teller (BET) measurements. 
The pore size distribution (PSD) was plotted by applying a non-local 
density functional theory (DFT) method. A JSM-6700F scanning elec -
tron microscope (SEM; JEOL, Tokyo, Japan) was used to inspect the 
morphologies of the AC samples. Raman spectroscopy was conducted 
with a Bruker spectrometer (Bruker Corporation, Germany) with an 
excitation wavelength of 532 nm to study the microstructures of the AC 
samples. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, ESCALAB 250Xi, 
Thermo Fisher, USA) was conducted using a monochromatic Al- K
α 
source. 
2.4. Preparation of electrodes 
The preparation method for the working electrode involved the 
following steps. First, AC (80 wt%) was mixed with acetylene black 
( > 99.9%, 10 wt%) and poly(vinylidene fluoride) (PVDF, Sigma-Aldrich, 
10 wt%) in N -methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP, Sigma-Aldrich) to obtain a 
homogeneous mixture. Second, the paste-like mixture was uniformly 
coated on Ni foam of dimensions 1 × 1 cm
2
. Third, the resulting elec -
trode (with a mass loading of active material of approximately 2.4 mg) 
was dried in a vacuum oven at 80 
◦
C for 24 h. 
2.5. Electrochemical measurements 
Electrochemical experiments were carried out with an electro -
chemical workstation (CHI 660E, Shanghai, China) to assess the relevant 
properties of the AC samples. The test conditions were as follows: con -
ventional three-electrode system with 6 M aqueous KOH solution as the 
electrolyte, a platinum sheet as the counter electrode, and a saturated 
calomel electrode (SCE) as the reference. Cyclic voltammetry (CV) tests 
were conducted at scanning rates of 1, 2, 5, and 10 mV s
� 1
. Galvano -
static charge – discharge (GCD) measurements were made at current 
densities of 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, and 5 A g
� 1
. The potential window ranging 
from � 1.0 V to 0 V was selected for CV and GCD tests. Electrochemical 
impedance spectra (EIS) were obtained in the frequency range 100

3. Results and discussion 
3.1. Characterization of carbon materials 
Fig. 1 shows the N
2

relative pressures below 0.1 P/P

be seen in Fig. 1 (a), compared with C/600 
◦

◦
C, relatively 
obvious hysteresis loops with typical characteristics of type IV isotherms 
were observed for C/500 
◦
C and C/700 
◦

surface areas and pore structure parameters of the AC samples. C/600 
◦
C 
displayed the highest specific surface area (2074.72 m
2 
g

largest total pore volume (0.930 cm
3 
g

1033.38 m

cm

, respectively. It is generally acknowledged that the electro -
chemical performance of a supercapacitor not only depends on its spe -
cific surface area, but also its pore framework (porosity and PSD). PSD 
plots of the AC samples obtained at different pyrolysis temperatures are 
shown in Fig. 1 (b). C/600 
◦
C displayed a smooth curve with the pore size 
centered at around 2 nm, implying that such a micro/meso hierarchical 
porous structure is beneficial to achieve excellent performance in 
supercapacitors [ 41 ]. The micropore volume gradually decreased as the 
pyrolysis temperature was increased from 600 
◦
C to 800 
◦
C due to 
collapse or amalgamation of the micropore structure [ 42 , 43 ]. Further -
more, the order of average pore diameters can be seen in Table 1 ; 
C/800 
◦
C (2.56 nm) > C/700 
◦
C (2.10 nm) > C/600 
◦
C (1.79 nm). Other 
data related to mesopore area and the average diameters of mesopores 
are collected in Table S1 . 
The surface morphologies of the AC samples characterized by SEM 
are shown in Fig. 2 . It can be seen that C/500 
◦
C was composed of a large 
number of diffuse spherical particles [ Fig. 2 (a)]. When the pyrolysis 
temperature was increased to 600 
◦
C, a fluffy Hemistepta lyrata -like 
structure with abundant pores was observed [ Fig. 2 (b)]. The presence of 
a large number of micropores ( < 2 nm) contributes to a high specific 
surface area, which is beneficial for high electrical double-layer capac -
itance due to abundant adsorption sites for ions [ 44 ]. Mesopores (2 – 50 
nm) allow ions to easily access inner micropores by shortening their 
diffusion distance and reducing diffusion resistance [ 45 ]. Moreover, a 
small number of macropores ( > 50 nm) favor ion transport as 
ion-buffering reservoirs [ 46 , 47 ]. On further increasing the pyrolysis 
temperature to 700 
◦
C and 800 
◦
C, the fluffy Hemistepta lyrata -like 
structure disappeared, being replaced by clusters or chunks of spherical 
particles [ Fig. 2 (c and d)]. These observations are consistent with the 
BET results. 
Additionally, Raman measurements were carried out to further 
validate the structures of C/500 
◦
C, C/600 
◦
C, C/700 
◦
C, and C/800 
◦
C 
( Fig. 3 ). Two prominent D-band and G-band peaks due to amorphous 
carbon were seen for all of the samples. The D-band (ca. 1340 cm
� 1
) can 
be attributed to disorder or defects in a graphitic structure with A 1
g 
symmetry. The G-band (ca. 1590 cm
� 1
) corresponds to an in-plane 
stretching vibration of sp
2 
bonds of carbon in the graphite lattice 
mode E
2g 
[ 44 , 48 ]. The intensity ratio of the D- and G-bands (I
D
/I
G
) is 
often used to represent the degree of disorder or defects in carbon ma -
terials. A higher ratio reflects a lower degree of graphitization [ 48 , 49 ]. 
The Raman spectra ( Fig. 3 ) indicated partial graphite characteristics for 
all four samples. C/500 
◦
C displayed the highest intensity ratio (I
D
/I
G 
=
1.95), reflecting the lowest degree of graphitization and the highest 
content of disordered carbon material. This observation was consistent 
with the SEM image [ Fig. 2 (a)]. The I
D
/I
G 
values of C/600 
◦
C, C/700 
◦
C, 
and C/800 
◦
C were 1.65, 1.58, and 1.62, respectively, suggesting that 
the AC samples prepared at higher temperatures possessed higher de -
grees of graphitization and excellent electronic conductivity. Moreover, 
there were no significant changes in the I
D
/I
G 
ratio when the pyrolysis 
temperature exceeded 600 
◦
C. Therefore, based on the above analysis, 
600 
◦
C was identified as an appropriate pyrolysis temperature for pre -
paring high-performance carbon-based electrodes, and C/600 
◦
C was 
selected for further studies.
